subject: design-technology
title: Modelling
final_note: You worked through the key terms in Modelling.

concepts.def: Forming and refining ideas in the mind or as simple representations to explore how a design might work in principle.
Two-dimensional and three-dimensional drawings, such as sketches, perspective and orthographic views, used to develop and communicate design ideas.
A tangible three-dimensional model, often scaled or made in cheaper materials, used to test the form, proportion or function of a design.
Software used to create accurate virtual two-dimensional and three-dimensional models that can be modified, analysed and shared quickly and easily.
Producing physical parts directly from CAD data, for example by 3D printing, so that designs can be evaluated quickly.
A physical model made proportionally smaller or larger than the real product, with every dimension reduced or enlarged by the same ratio.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Modelling — a core area of Design Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Modelling brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Modelling.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: The main purpose of modelling in design is to:
options: Test and communicate design ideas cheaply before committing to production
Replace the need for any final product
Decorate the design studio
Delay the project as long as possible

mcqs.q: A key advantage of CAD modelling over physical modelling is:
options: It never contains any errors
Designs can be modified and virtually tested without consuming physical material
It requires no computer skills
It always costs more than physical models

mcqs.q: Rapid prototyping is best described as:
options: Sketching very quickly with a pen
Building production tooling for mass manufacture
Producing physical parts directly from CAD data, for example by 3D printing
Interviewing users about a concept

mcqs.q: What is the difference between an aesthetic model and a functional prototype?
options: There is no difference between them
An aesthetic model tests how it works; a functional prototype tests how it looks
Both are only ever made at full size
An aesthetic model shows look and form; a functional prototype tests how the design works

mcqs.q: Must a model be a full-size working version of the product?
options: No - models can be sketches, virtual CAD files or simple scaled forms; each type only needs enough detail to answer the design question being asked.
1:5 means the model took five hours to build.
Yes - models must always be made of the final material.
Yes - a model only counts if it is full-size and fully working.

mcqs.q: Has CAD made physical modelling unnecessary?
options: Yes - physical models are now illegal in commercial design.
1:5 means the model took five hours to build.
Yes - everything a physical model shows can be seen on screen.
No - CAD is powerful for accuracy and virtual testing, but physical models are still needed to judge ergonomics, feel, weight and real user interaction.

mcqs.q: In a 1:5 scale model, is the model five times bigger than the product?
options: 1:5 means the model took five hours to build.
Yes - physical models are now illegal in commercial design.
Yes - the second number says how many times bigger the model is.
No - 1:5 means one unit on the model represents five on the product, so the model is one fifth of the real size.

sequence.def: Lowest fidelity: the idea expressed in words or thought
Sketches and diagrams put the concept on paper
Cheap materials show form and scale, no function
A functional model proves the design operates
Final materials and processes, ready to validate production
